title: Orient: destroy the wrong model, act from the better one
tagline: What model of the situation should I currently act from, and what should I do next to test or exploit that model?
principle: The purpose of an OODA loop is not to move through four boxes quickly. It is to maintain an orientation that survives contact with reality, act coherently from that orientation, and use the consequences of action to construct a better one when it fails.

operations.label: Negate an assumption
operations.challenge: What if the opposite of this were true?

operations.label: Remove an assumption
operations.challenge: What does the model look like with this assumption deleted?

operations.label: Ask what evidence actually supports it
operations.challenge: Which observation, not inference, supports this?

operations.label: Ask what would remain true without it
operations.challenge: What would still be true if this assumption were gone?

operations.label: Remove the goal
operations.challenge: What changes if the goal disappears?

operations.label: Invert the goal
operations.challenge: What would you do if you were trying to cause the opposite?

operations.label: Ask whether the goal belongs to a different game
operations.challenge: Is this goal left over from a game you are no longer playing?

operations.label: Ask what changes if continuing to play is not mandatory
operations.challenge: What becomes possible if you are allowed to stop playing?

operations.label: Widen the system boundary
operations.challenge: What lies just outside this boundary that still shapes the outcome?

operations.label: Narrow the system boundary
operations.challenge: Which part of this boundary actually matters now?

operations.label: Move the competitive boundary
operations.challenge: Why is this the boundary? Who else competes for the same need?

operations.label: Add a previously external actor
operations.challenge: Who outside the current picture affects the result?

operations.label: Remove an irrelevant actor
operations.challenge: Which actor could you leave out without losing anything that matters?

operations.label: Delete a category
operations.challenge: What do you see if this label did not exist?

operations.label: Merge two categories
operations.challenge: What if these two kinds were treated as one?

operations.label: Split one category
operations.challenge: Which different things are hiding under this one label?

operations.label: Ask whether the labels carve reality at useful joints
operations.challenge: Do these labels follow differences that change what you would do?

operations.label: Reverse actor roles
operations.challenge: What if the one you think is reacting is actually leading?

operations.label: Split an apparent single actor into several
operations.challenge: Is this one actor, or several with different incentives?

operations.label: Merge actors with aligned incentives
operations.challenge: Do these actors effectively want the same thing?

operations.label: Reinterpret who has initiative
operations.challenge: Who is actually setting the pace here?

operations.label: Detach an object from its intended function
operations.challenge: What property matters independently of the object's normal function?

operations.label: Ask what properties it has independently of its name
operations.challenge: Describe it without its name: what is it physically, or what can it do?

operations.label: Assign it a new role
operations.challenge: What job could this do that nobody has asked it to do?

operations.label: Combine properties from several objects
operations.challenge: What new thing do these properties make together?

operations.label: Treat a constraint as a resource
operations.challenge: How could this limit work in your favour?

operations.label: Test whether a constraint is actually fixed
operations.challenge: What would show this constraint is negotiable?

operations.label: Move the constraint elsewhere
operations.challenge: Could this limit bind somewhere it costs less?

operations.label: Change time scale
operations.challenge: Is this still a constraint over a week, or over five years?

operations.label: Reverse a causal arrow
operations.challenge: What if the effect is causing the cause?

operations.label: Remove a causal link
operations.challenge: What if these two things are not connected at all?

operations.label: Introduce a common cause
operations.challenge: What third thing could produce both?

operations.label: Ask whether the relation is merely correlated
operations.challenge: Have you seen one change the other, or only seen them together?

operations.label: Remove an information source
operations.challenge: What would you conclude without this signal? (The observation stays in the ledger.)

operations.label: Ask what happens if the signal is wrong
operations.challenge: If this signal were misleading, what would you do differently?

operations.label: Ask what important signal is systematically absent
operations.challenge: What would you expect to see that you never see?

operations.label: Slow down deliberately
operations.challenge: What would you notice if you took one more observation before acting?

operations.label: Compress deliberation deliberately
operations.challenge: What is the smallest action that would teach you something today?

operations.label: Ask whether speed is compensating for poor orientation
operations.challenge: Are you acting faster to avoid admitting the model is wrong?

guided.why: A contradiction is open: challenge the causal model.
Every candidate shares one boundary: challenge the boundary.
Actions keep failing: challenge the link between model and action.
Nothing could weaken this orientation: challenge its testability.
A constraint has not been tested as fixed.
An item it depends on is marked stale.
Tempo is high while results are getting worse.
Objects are tied to their usual functions.
No visible weakness: start with the usual suspects.

jolts.prompt: Pretend the person you are trying to influence is the one running the plan. What are they doing to you?
Name your tightest limit. Now design the move that only works because of it.
Pick the dullest resource you have. Give it a job that would surprise its owner.
Suppose you were allowed to walk away from this tomorrow. What would you still want to keep?
Cut the situation down to the one interaction that would matter if everything else stayed the same.
List one thing you would expect to hear, see or measure if your model were right, and have never heard.
Find one thing happening in the background that could produce both what you see and what you fear.
If you had to act within the hour, what would you do, and what would it tell you?

creation.label: new boundary + overlooked signal
creation.text: What orientation appears if you combine the boundary “{a}” with the observation “{b}”?

creation.label: constraint → resource
creation.text: If “{a}” is a resource rather than a limit, what does it let you do about “{b}”?

creation.label: object + alternative function
creation.text: What can you build from “{a}” together with “{b}”?

creation.label: actor + alternative role
creation.text: If “{a}”, how does that change what “{b}” means?

creation.label: intent + unexplained observation
creation.text: What does “{b}” suggest about how to pursue “{a}”?

creation.label: removed assumption + existing capability
creation.text: Without the old assumption, and with “{a}”, what could “{b}” now do?

dimensions.label: Observations explained
dimensions.question: What already makes sense under this model?

dimensions.label: Assumptions
dimensions.question: What has to be true for this model to work?

dimensions.label: Moves opened
dimensions.question: What becomes possible under this model?

dimensions.label: Reversibility
dimensions.question: Can its next test be cheaply reversed?

dimensions.label: Cost of error
dimensions.question: What happens if this model is wrong?

dimensions.label: Information speed
dimensions.question: How quickly can reality discriminate it?

triggers.label: No useful action follows from the model
High tempo but getting worse results
New information breaks a central causal claim

diagnostics.title: Rewording
diagnostics.message: You changed the wording, not the orientation.

diagnostics.title: Boundary lock
diagnostics.message: Every candidate preserves the same system boundary.

diagnostics.title: Untestable model
diagnostics.message: You have not identified an observation that could weaken this orientation.

diagnostics.title: Tempo substitution
diagnostics.message: You are increasing action tempo without changing the orientation that produced repeated failures.

diagnostics.title: Immutable-constraint assumption
diagnostics.message: This constraint has not yet been tested as genuinely fixed.

diagnostics.title: Low-information action
diagnostics.message: This action appears to produce little information about which orientation is better.

diagnostics.title: Observation / inference collapse
diagnostics.message: This statement is currently labelled as an observation but contains an interpretation.

diagnostics.title: Prediction drift
diagnostics.message: The expected result changed after the outcome was known.

diagnostics.title: Untraced action
diagnostics.message: This action is not connected to an existing orientation.

actionTypes.label: Maneuver
actionTypes.help: Changes the situation while keeping meaningful flexibility.

actionTypes.label: Commitment
actionTypes.help: Expensive or difficult to reverse. Needs a stronger orientation and a clear reconsideration trigger.

actionTypes.label: Wait / watch
actionTypes.help: Deliberately keeps options open while gathering more reality signals. Not indecision.

modes.label: Other agent / adversary
prompts: Who has the initiative right now?
What can the other actor observe of you?
What does the other actor expect you to do?
Could what you see be a deliberate appearance?
When would your move matter most to them?
How else could their behaviour be read?

modes.label: Coordination / team
prompts: Does everyone hold the same picture of the situation?
Who knows something the others do not?

worksheet: What are you currently inferring from it?
What does that model fail to explain?
Which assumption, boundary, goal or object-function can be challenged?
What would you expect to observe if it were useful?
What result would cause you to reconsider?

why.title: Orientation is the centre, not step two
why.text: Boyd's later briefings draw orientation as the part of the loop that shapes what gets observed, which decisions look available and how results are read. This page therefore makes the model you act from the main workspace, and treats observe, decide and act as what feeds and tests it.

why.title: Destroy, then create
why.text: In Destruction and Creation Boyd argues that a concept turned inward on itself drifts out of step with reality, so it has to be broken into parts and the parts recombined into a new concept that fits what is observed. Here that is concrete: each destructive move names what it challenges and requires a replacement, and every candidate cites the fragments it was built from.

why.title: Faster action does not repair a faulty orientation
why.text: Tempo matters, but a fast loop run from the wrong model just produces wrong actions sooner. The page lets you set tempo, compresses prompts when it is high, and warns when tempo rises while failures repeat under an unchanged orientation.

why.title: Observations and interpretations are kept apart
why.text: Every item is typed as observed, inferred or unknown. An inference cannot be relabelled as an observation; promoting it records a separate observation. Doubtful observations are qualified, never deleted.

why.title: Orientations stay provisional
why.text: Candidates are never declared winners. You adopt one provisionally, rejected candidates stay in the lineage, and confidence is shown next to its evidence rather than standing in for it. There is no score.

why.title: Reality, not this page, discriminates models
why.text: The page cannot tell you which orientation is right. It asks for a prediction before you act, freezes it when the action starts, and puts it next to what actually happened.

how: Write down what you have actually observed, what you infer from it, and what you do not know.
State the model you are currently acting from, with its boundary, assumptions and a prediction.
Test it. If nothing argues against it, keep acting from it and observe.
If it is stale, contradicted or unproductive, reorient: make one to three concrete destructive moves, each with a replacement.
Build two to four candidate orientations from the fragments, contrast them, and adopt one provisionally.
Choose one next action that follows from it, with an expected signal and a reason to reconsider. Starting the action freezes the prediction.
Record what happened next to what you expected, then return to orientation.

rao.title: When should you redraw the map?
rao.text: If ordinary corrections keep failing, the problem may no longer be your position on the map. The map itself may be wrong. Routine feedback adjusts the action; reorientation interrupts the routine and changes the model.
rao.basis: Interpretation drawing on Rao's reading of orientation as the part of the loop that generates interrupts and exceptional course corrections, while observe, decide and act run in sequence.

rao.title: Tempo is not just speed
rao.text: Tempo is about timing relative to how the situation unfolds, not maximising the number of loops. Sometimes the right tempo is slower.
rao.basis: Interpretation drawing on Rao's book Tempo and his argument that operating faster is not universally better.

rao.title: Analysis or tinkering?
rao.text: When goals and plans keep failing, cheap exploratory moves can find what analysis cannot, by breaking assumptions about how resources can be used. A probe is a small, deliberate piece of tinkering.
rao.basis: Interpretation drawing on Rao's essay contrasting goal-driven problem solving with serendipitous tinkering.

rao.title: When the roadmap keeps slipping
rao.text: A plan that keeps missing may be a symptom of uncertainty, not of a poor plan. More detail can hide the open question instead of answering it.
rao.basis: This page's interpretation, in the spirit of Rao's critique of goal-driven planning; Rao does not make this exact claim about project plans.

rao.title: Destruction is a means
rao.text: Breaking a model apart is useful only if the replacement changes what you can see, expect or do. Destruction without a replacement is not progress.
rao.basis: This page's interpretation of Boyd's Destruction and Creation; the Rao essays are listed for his broader reading of Boyd.

boyd.label: Boyd
boyd.about: Ideas attributed to John Boyd: OODA; orientation; destruction and creation; feedback and reorientation; synthesis; tempo. Paraphrased, not quoted.

rao.label: Rao
rao.about: Interpretations and extensions from Venkatesh Rao's writing on tempo, tinkering, model revision and the misuse of OODA, each marked as an interpretation.

teo.label: Yu Jie Teo
teo.about: Examples, applications and vocabulary from Yu Jie Teo's notes, OODA, Orientation, and Slouching. Applications of the ideas, not quotations from Boyd.

page.label: This page
page.about: Design choices made for this planner.

cards.title: Nakatomi Space
cards.lesson: Repurpose overlooked features of the environment.
cards.text: When an opponent controls every obvious exit and passage, look for what they are not watching, such as ventilation ducts. The environment can be used in ways it was not built for.
cards.seed: Someone controls every obvious route to what I need

cards.title: Monster Chess
cards.text: In monster chess one side moves twice per turn and can hold off a large material advantage for a while. Timing can offset resources, but only temporarily.
cards.seed: I have fewer resources but can move faster

cards.title: Reality Signal
cards.text: Running the loop needs a reality signal, not full situational awareness. Ask which single signal is enough to tell you whether the model holds.
cards.seed: I am waiting for complete information before acting

cards.title: Map and Territory
cards.text: The map is not the territory: a model is always incomplete. Look for where the model and the system you are acting on disagree.
cards.seed: My model keeps disagreeing with what happens

cards.title: Boundary Definition
cards.text: The right boundary carves reality at its joints, cutting away irrelevant stimuli and focusing attention where it matters most.
cards.seed: I am not sure what the situation actually includes

cards.title: Object Function
cards.text: Objects and agents are not limited to their intended functions. Recombining them can open strategies outside the usual limits.
cards.seed: I am stuck using my tools the usual way

cards.title: Overprepared Adversary
cards.lesson: Avoid the domain where preparation is strongest.
cards.text: Do not attack where the other side is already heavily prepared; look where their orientation, preparation or awareness is weaker.
cards.seed: I keep competing where the other side is strongest

cards.title: Deep Memory
cards.text: Keeping a memory of past patterns stops you repeating an orientation that has already failed. This planner checks new candidates against weakened assumptions from earlier loops.
cards.seed: This feels like a problem I have failed at before

cards.title: Perception Reorientation
cards.text: People act on what they perceive, not on objective reality. Changing what someone can observe can change what they do, without changing material conditions.
cards.seed: Someone else's behaviour does not match the facts as I see them

cards.title: Tempo vs Orientation
cards.lesson: Faster execution does not repair a bad model.
cards.text: High tempo with an inferior orientation can lose to a slower tempo with a better one. Check the model before speeding up.
cards.seed: I am working faster and results are not improving

examples.title: A stalled project
examples.purpose: Everyday orientation: a full reality → orientation → action → observation chain.
examples.note: A mundane illustrative case written for this page.

steps.title: My project keeps slipping even though I spend more time planning it
steps.description: A research and software project that keeps missing its dates.

steps.text: Ship the next usable version of the project
The last three plans each missed their dates
Work expanded beyond each plan's estimate
Planning time doubled over two months and throughput did not rise
I need a better plan
The problem is insufficient planning quality
About ten hours a week are available for the project
Which of the two possible directions for the next version is viable?

steps.matters: the level of detail in the plan
steps.observe: a more detailed plan will be met
steps.mechanism: insufficient plan detail causes the slips
steps.falsifier: A more detailed plan misses as badly as the earlier ones

steps.text: Previous increases in planning did not improve delivery

replacement.text: Uncertainty is too high for a detailed long-range plan to be useful

steps.inside: a high-uncertainty project where long-range plans hide the open questions
steps.explains: more planning did not improve delivery
steps.fails: whether execution capacity is also short
steps.keyAssumption: Uncertainty, not plan detail, is the bottleneck
steps.observe: one small artifact settles which of the two directions is viable
steps.move: Produce one small artifact or test that exposes the next uncertainty
steps.falsifier: The artifact shows the uncertainty was already low and execution capacity is the real constraint

steps.note: More planning did not help; testing the uncertainty is cheap.

steps.reason: Explained by O1: the bottleneck is uncertainty, not plan detail

steps.text: Produce one small artifact or test that exposes the next uncertainty
steps.expected: The result reveals which of the two possible directions is viable
steps.reconsider: The artifact reveals that the uncertainty was already low and execution capacity, not model uncertainty, is the actual constraint

consistency.discriminator: Whether a small artifact settles the choice between the two directions

steps.observed: A two-day prototype showed one direction fails on real data and the other works; it took two days, not the week I would have planned
steps.interpretation: The prediction held: testing the uncertainty settled the choice faster than planning around it.

predictions.result: One direction was ruled out by the prototype

examples.title: Southwest-style boundary reorientation
examples.purpose: Boundary destruction: the competitive boundary itself changes.
examples.note: An application from the author's OODA notes, modelled on Southwest Airlines; not a literal Boyd case study, and the details are illustrative.

steps.title: A new short-haul airline entering a crowded market
steps.description: A small airline deciding how to compete on short routes.

steps.text: Win enough passengers to sustain a small short-haul airline
Most trips on our routes are a few hundred kilometres long
Most people travelling between these cities drive or take the bus
Established airlines on these routes compete on service and schedule
Airlines flying the same routes
Our customers are people who already fly
Passengers choose between airlines on service and schedule
We are too small to match the incumbents' networks
A few aircraft and a simple point-to-point network

steps.inside: a new airline competing against established airlines
steps.matters: matching the incumbents on service and schedule
steps.observe: passengers switch from other airlines when our service is comparable
steps.move: Match the incumbents' service on a few routes
steps.falsifier: Passengers do not switch even when our service is comparable

steps.text: Most potential travellers on these routes are not flying at all

steps.challenge: Why is the relevant competitive boundary airlines?

replacement.text: Short-distance transport for the same journey: cars, buses and airlines
Our customers include people who currently drive or take the bus

steps.inside: a short-distance transport market where cars and buses are the main competition
steps.explains: most travellers on these routes are not flying
steps.fails: how the incumbent airlines will respond
steps.matters: a fare and frequency that beat driving or the bus door to door
steps.keyAssumption: Drivers and bus riders will fly if the trip is cheap and frequent enough
steps.observe: new passengers who previously drove or took the bus, not only passengers taken from other airlines
steps.move: Price and schedule one route against the car and the bus
steps.mechanism: travellers choose among modes for the same journey
steps.falsifier: New passengers come almost entirely from other airlines

steps.inside: a contest with the established airlines on these routes
steps.explains: established carriers dominate the routes we fly
steps.fails: why most travellers do not fly
steps.matters: matching the incumbents on service and schedule
steps.keyAssumption: We win passengers from other airlines
steps.observe: passengers switch from other airlines when service is comparable
steps.move: Match the incumbents' service on a few routes

steps.note: The contradiction is explained only once the boundary includes cars and buses.

steps.text: Offer a fare and timetable on one route priced against the cost of driving it
steps.expected: A large share of new passengers on that route previously drove or took the bus
steps.reconsider: New passengers come almost entirely from other airlines

consistency.discriminator: Where the new passengers on the route came from

examples.title: Boyd's snowmobile
examples.purpose: Destroy fixed object/function relationships and recombine the properties.
examples.note: Boyd's own illustration in Destruction and Creation (1976), paraphrased; the component list follows the author's notes.

steps.title: Getting across deep snow with what is at hand
steps.description: Four parts from four unrelated activities, and a need to travel over snow.

steps.text: Travel quickly over snow
Skis
Outboard motor
Bicycle handlebars
Tank tread
Skis are for a skier going down a slope
An outboard motor drives a boat
Handlebars steer a bicycle
Tank treads move a tank
Each object belongs to its own activity: slope, boat, bicycle, tank
None of these objects alone moves a person over deep snow

steps.inside: four unrelated objects, each defined by its usual job
steps.explains: why no single object solves the problem
steps.matters: finding the one object built for snow
steps.observe: no existing object will do the job
steps.move: Look for an existing snow vehicle
steps.mechanism: an object is what its usual function says it is

replacement.text: Skis: long low-friction runners that spread weight over snow
Outboard motor: a compact, portable source of power
Handlebars: a hand-held way to steer
Tank tread: grip and traction on soft ground
Snowmobile: runners to glide, a tread for traction, a motor for power and handlebars to steer

steps.inside: a design problem where parts can be recombined by their properties
steps.explains: why the answer was not any single existing object
steps.fails: whether the parts can be joined to bear the load
steps.keyAssumption: The properties survive being moved to a new machine
steps.observe: the assembled machine moves over snow under its own power and can be steered
steps.mechanism: properties detached from their usual functions can be recombined
steps.falsifier: The assembled machine cannot move or steer on snow

steps.note: Only the recombined properties explain how to cross the snow.

steps.text: Build a rough version and try it on a short stretch of snow
steps.expected: It moves under its own power and can be steered
steps.reconsider: It cannot move or steer on snow

consistency.discriminator: Whether the combined machine moves over snow
